fetched_contents.text: Spelling development throughout the elementary grades: The Dutch case Introduction It is generally assumed that the child's ability to spell is influenced by a variety of skills. Phonological skills appear to be critical (Gentry, 1982, Henderson and Beers, 1980) in addition to orthographic knowledge (Templeton & Morris, 2000), awareness of morphological structures (Treiman, Cassar, & Zukowski, 1994), and knowledge of spelling rules (Rittle-Johnson & Siegler, 1999). One popular conception of spelling development is that the skills and strategies that are acquired during the learning process follow a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages in which different sources of knowledge are used (Ehri, 1986, Ehri, 1992, Frith, 1980, Gentry, 1982, Henderson and Beers, 1980, Templeton and Bear, 1992). Both Gentry (1982) and Ehri, 1986, Ehri, 1992 have distinguished five stages for spelling development: (a) the precommunicative stage, (b) the semiphonetic stage, (c) the phonetic stage, (d) the transitional or morphemic stage, and (e) the correct stage. Each stage is labeled such that it reflects the predominant information and strategies used at that stage of development. It is suggested that children initially combine letters and letter like symbols in a relatively haphazard manner without showing systematic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences. During the second stage of spelling development, children use their knowledge of letter names to spell, but their written word representations do not yet constitute a complete mapping of the sound structures of words. The sound-out strategy is considered characteristic of the third spelling stage: All of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but the children do not show full knowledge of orthographic conventions. In the fourth spelling stage, children demonstrate their growing knowledge of basic spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations in their spellings. Finally, children enter the fifth stage of spelling development when both the phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects of spelling competence are mastered. Other theories that postulate spelling development to occur in a stage-like manner have clear synergies with that of Gentry (1982) and Ehri, 1986, Ehri, 1992, but have posited the existence of slightly different stages. For instance, Templeton and Bear (1992) and Henderson (1992) have extended the phonetic and transitional stages to describe different phonological and orthographic characteristics within words, across syllables, and across morphemes. In addition, some stage theories do not subsume a qualitatively different “correct” stage, recognizing that correctly spelled words are not necessarily spelled using qualitatively different information and strategies from incorrectly spelled words. All stage theories, however, presume a transition from relying on phonological properties of words to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules. Furthermore, the different stage theories have the common feature that the stages of development are qualified by the static and consistent use of one single strategy to solve the spelling problem. Stage theories, thus, conceptualize transitions from one stage to another as instant qualitative changes in the use of strategy and involve children to spell words fundamentally differently in the successive stages of spelling. According to stage theory, therefore, the development of spelling ability should be conceived as a discontinuous and multidimensional process, reflecting instant developmental changes in children's information and strategy use. Theories that conceive spelling development as proceeding through a series of distinct stages are not without controversy. It can be argued, for instance, that a stage description of spelling development does not fully capture the complexity of learning to spell. More importantly, the depth of children's knowledge of the spelling system of a language and the variety of knowledge sources and strategies that children can use to spell are not taken into account within such a stage approach to the development of spelling (Treiman and Cassar, 1997, Varnhagen et al., 1997). Therefore, some researchers have suggested that the variability of strategy use in spelling may be better described in terms of the general learning framework of overlapping waves as proposed by Siegler (2000). In essence, the theory of overlapping waves is based upon three key components: (a) abundant variability, (b) adaptive choice, and (c) gradual change. During the learning process, that is, children develop a broad repertoire of spelling strategies where they can adaptively choose from at given times in the development (Bowman and Treiman, 2002, Rittle-Johnson and Siegler, 1999), but over time, gradual changes in the frequency of the use of particular strategies may occur (Steffler, Varnhagen, Friesen & Treiman, 1998; Varnhagen et al, 1997). The overlapping waves model, thus, endorses the use of multiple strategies to problem-solving and shifts in strategy performance, but clearly denies the consistent and static use of only a single strategy at a particular point in the development of children's spelling ability. According to overlapping waves theory, therefore, the development of spelling ability should be conceived as a continuous and unidimensional process, reflecting gradual improvements in children's phonological, orthographic, and morphological knowledge. The discrepancies between the stage and overlapping wave approaches to children's spelling development raise the question of whether spelling ability should be conceptualized as a multidimensional or unidimensional phenomenon. fetched_contents.text: Stages, Phases, Repertoires, and Waves: Learning to Spell and Read Words - Templeton - 2020 - The Reading Teacher Feature Article First published: 19 October 2020 Abstract Competing theories are quite common in education. In spelling research, two general perspectives have emerged over the years: stage theory and repertoire/alternative theories. Exploring these perspectives is important because teachers need to understand how spelling knowledge is critical for learning to read words and to write them. Stage theory suggests that learners follow a developmental progression that reflects the increasing complexity of the spelling system itself. Alternative theorists suggest that learners do not follow a linear progression but are able to understand much more information about the spelling system throughout their development. The author explores the debate between these two conceptions, identifying not only important differences but also where there is common ground. Implications for spelling, word analysis, and vocabulary instruction are provided. References More to Explore Citing Literature

## Core developmental spelling model mini-report

The developmental spelling model presented in the evidence is broadly stage-based, with several authors identifying a five-stage progression. One source states that children progress through five stages of spelling development, from precommunicative through invented spelling to accurate dictionary spelling [N1-R1]. Another source explicitly names the same five-phase sequence: precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional, and correct [N1-R2]. A third source also lists the five stages as precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional, and correct [N1-R3], while a fourth source describes the Bear, Invernizzi, Templeton & Johnston model as an overview of the five stages [N1-R4]. A fifth source notes that Gentry’s model also outlines a five-phase progression [N1-R5]. Across these sources, the core model is therefore best summarized as a five-stage developmental sequence.

### Which stages are recognized in the model?

The most consistent stage sequence across the evidence is:

1. **Precommunicative stage**  
2. **Semiphonetic stage**  
3. **Phonetic stage**  
4. **Transitional or morphemic stage**  
5. **Correct stage** [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]

Some sources use slightly different phrasing, such as “emergent invented spelling” instead of “precommunicative” [N1-R1], and some describe the final stage as “dictionary” spelling or the “correct stage” [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The empirical Dutch study also notes that both Gentry (1982) and Ehri, 1986, 1992 have distinguished these five stages [N1-F1].

### What each stage represents developmentally

Each stage marks a qualitative shift in how children represent spelling and use spelling knowledge:

- **Precommunicative stage**: Children combine letters and letter-like symbols in a relatively haphazard manner without systematic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences [N1-F1].  
- **Semiphonetic stage**: Children use knowledge of letter names to spell, but their written word representations do not yet constitute a complete mapping of the sound structures of words [N1-F1].  
- **Phonetic stage**: The sound-out strategy is characteristic: all of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but children do not yet show full knowledge of orthographic conventions [N1-F1].  
- **Transitional/morphemic stage**: Children demonstrate growing knowledge of basic spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations in their spellings [N1-F1].  
- **Correct stage**: Children master phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects of spelling competence [N1-F1].  

This developmental sequence reflects increasing sophistication: from arbitrary mark-making through letter-name use, to phonetic spelling, to spelling that incorporates patterns, conventions, and morphology, and finally to conventional, rule-based spelling [N1-F1].

### How the model explains transitions between stages

The stage model explains transitions as qualitative changes in the use of strategy and information. In the precommunicative stage, children rely on arbitrary or haphazard letter combinations, whereas later stages become increasingly systematic [N1-F1]. Stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also says that transitions are conceptualized as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].  

A key theoretical point is that each stage is labeled by the predominant information and strategies used at that stage [N1-F1]. This means the model does not treat spelling as a smooth, linear increase in accuracy alone, but as a sequence of qualitatively distinct phases where different knowledge sources and strategies dominate [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that some stage theories do not subsume a qualitatively different “correct” stage, recognizing that correctly spelled words are not necessarily spelled using qualitatively different information and strategies [N1-F1]. Still, the common core of stage theory is a transition from phonological dependence toward orthographic and morphological mastery [N1-F1].

### Theoretical context

The evidence also emphasizes that stage theory is one of several perspectives in spelling research. The 2020 article on spelling and reading contrasts stage theory with repertoire/alternative theories, noting that stage theory suggests learners follow a developmental progression reflecting increasing complexity of the spelling system itself, whereas repertoire theories suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand more information throughout development [N5-F2]. This distinction is important because it shows that the developmental spelling model is not the only explanatory framework, and that stage theory is debated in the literature [N5-F2].  

Overall, the core developmental spelling model is a five-stage sequence: precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional/morphemic, and correct. Each stage represents a qualitative shift in spelling strategy and knowledge use, with transitions reflecting discontinuous, multidimensional developmental changes [N1-F1]. The model is supported by the repeated identification of these stages across sources, but the evidence also shows that it is contested by alternative views [N1-F1][N5-F2].

## Early spelling development mini-report

### How letter-name and letter-sound knowledge emerge

Early spelling development begins with children learning to associate letter names with sounds. The evidence states that children progress through stages where knowledge of letter names and letter-sound correspondences becomes central [N1-F1]. One source explicitly notes that during the second stage of spelling development, children use knowledge of letter names to spell, but their written word representations do not yet fully map sound structures [N1-F1]. Another source describes the Bear, Invernizzi, Templeton & Johnston model as an overview of the five stages of spelling development, which implies that letter-name and letter-sound knowledge are foundational to the earliest stages [N1-R4]. A separate source on early spelling development also notes that children start making marks and scribbles at around 1–2 years old, and that prephonological and phonological stages are early parts of this process [N2-R5].  

This suggests that letter-name knowledge emerges before letter-sound knowledge becomes systematic. In the semiphonetic stage, letter names are used, but the mapping to sound is incomplete [N1-F1]. Later, as phonetic spelling develops, children begin to represent more of the sound structure of words [N1-F1]. So the progression is from name-based mark-making to more sound-based spelling [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### What early spelling attempts look like

Early spelling attempts are described as invented spelling and mark-making. One source says children progress from precommunicative through invented spelling to accurate dictionary spelling [N1-R1]. Another source similarly describes the five stages as including invented spelling [N1-R2][N1-R3]. The same evidence describes the precommunicative stage as combining letters and letter-like symbols in a relatively haphazard manner [N1-F1]. A separate early-spelling source says children start making marks and scribbles on surfaces at around 1–2 years old, and that mark-making “make meaning” [N2-R5].  

In the semiphonetic stage, children use letter names to spell, but their spellings do not yet fully represent word sounds [N1-F1]. In the phonetic stage, the sound-out strategy is characteristic: all of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but orthographic conventions are still not fully mastered [N1-F1]. So early spelling attempts can range from arbitrary scribbles and invented spellings through increasingly sound-driven but still inconsistent spellings [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R5].

### Why children struggle with early spelling

Children struggle with early spelling because their spelling systems are still developing and not yet fully aligned with the conventions of the writing system. In the precommunicative stage, letter combinations are arbitrary and lack systematic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences [N1-F1]. In the semiphonetic stage, children use letter names, but their written representations do not yet map sound structures fully [N1-F1]. In the phonetic stage, they can represent all sounds, but orthographic conventions remain weak [N1-F1].  

The evidence also notes that some stage theories do not subsume a qualitatively different “correct” stage, recognizing that correctly spelled words are not necessarily spelled using qualitatively different information and strategies from incorrectly spelled words [N1-F1]. This implies that early spelling struggles are not just about getting the right letters, but about coordinating multiple knowledge sources—letter names, sounds, and orthographic conventions—that children are still learning to integrate [N1-F1].  

In short, early spelling struggles stem from incomplete knowledge of letter-sound correspondences, inconsistent use of letter names, and limited orthographic awareness [N1-F1][N2-R5]. These limitations are developmentally normal and reflect the transition from precommunicative mark-making to more systematic spelling [N1-R1][N1-F1].

## Intermediate spelling development mini-report

### How phonetic spelling emerges and evolves

Phonetic spelling emerges as children begin to represent the sounds of words more systematically. The evidence states that the sound-out strategy is characteristic of the third spelling stage: all of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but children do not yet show full knowledge of orthographic conventions [N1-F1]. A related source says that during the phonetic stage, children between the ages of 5–7 have a better understanding of phonetics and can spell words based on that understanding [N3-R2].  

This means phonetic spelling develops from semiphonetic letter-name use to a more consistent, if still imperfect, representation of sounds. It is not yet fully conventional spelling, but it reflects a qualitative shift toward sound-based word representation [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that phonetic spelling is part of a broader developmental sequence that eventually includes spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphology [N1-F1].

### What spelling patterns children begin to use

As spelling moves beyond phonetic stage, children begin to use spelling patterns rather than relying solely on sound-out strategies. The evidence describes the transitional or morphemic stage as one where children demonstrate growing knowledge of basic spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations in their spellings [N1-F1]. A separate source identifies the stage sequence as including patterns within-words and syllable juncture [N3-R3]. Another source notes that teaching spelling of specific patterns and groups is more effective than testing mixed patterns for a single sound or phonetically [N3-R5].  

This suggests that intermediate spelling development involves learning common letter patterns and morphological structures. Children start to recognize recurring spellings and the relationships between word parts, such as prefixes, suffixes, and base words [N1-F1][N3-R3]. These patterns are not yet fully conventionalized, but they represent a shift from sound-driven spelling to rule-like or pattern-based spelling [N1-F1][N3-R5].

### How accuracy and consistency improve

Accuracy and consistency improve as children move from phonetic spelling toward transitional/morphemic spelling. In the phonetic stage, children represent all sounds, but orthographic conventions are still weak [N1-F1]. In the transitional stage, children begin to show more consistent use of spelling patterns and orthographic conventions [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that longitudinal studies of spelling development are relevant because they examine how spelling skills change over time [N6-R3].  

This implies that accuracy and consistency do not improve uniformly. Children may initially produce many phonetically plausible but incorrect spellings, and then gradually integrate more conventional spellings and patterns [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The empirical evidence also supports a developmental sequence in which spelling becomes more systematic and less arbitrary as children gain more knowledge of spelling patterns and orthographic rules [N6-R3][N1-F1].

### Summary

Intermediate spelling development is marked by the emergence of phonetic spelling, followed by the use of spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphology. Accuracy and consistency improve as children move from sound-based spelling toward pattern-based and rule-based spelling [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R3]. The evidence supports a progressive shift from phonetic representation to more systematic spelling strategies [N1-F1].

## Late spelling development mini-report

### How conventional spelling emerges and becomes dominant

Conventional spelling becomes dominant as children move into the transitional/morphemic and correct stages. The evidence states that the transitional stage demonstrates growing knowledge of spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations [N1-F1]. The correct stage is described as when phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects of spelling competence are mastered [N1-F1]. A related source notes that the transitional stage reflects an emerging understanding of conventional spelling patterns and phonics rules, with vowels being a particular focus [N4-R4].  

This means conventional spelling emerges gradually, not suddenly. It becomes dominant as children internalize orthographic rules and use them alongside morphological knowledge [N1-F1][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that spelling becomes more accurate and conventional as children move from phonetic to transitional spelling [N1-F1]. In other words, late spelling is characterized by the increasing use of established spelling conventions rather than arbitrary or purely phonetic spellings [N1-F1][N4-R4].

### What spelling rules children learn

Children learn spelling rules related to orthography, morphology, and phonics. The evidence notes that the transitional stage involves growing knowledge of spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations [N1-F1]. It also says that the correct stage is when phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects are mastered [N1-F1]. A separate source on late spelling development states that the transitional stage reflects an emerging understanding of conventional spelling patterns and phonics rules [N4-R4].  

These rules include both surface orthographic conventions and deeper morphological rules. Children learn to apply rules for silent letters, doubling consonants, vowel patterns, and word parts [N1-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that spelling knowledge is not limited to one source; it includes phonological, orthographic, and morphological information [N5-F2]. This supports the idea that late spelling is not just about memorizing isolated rules, but about using a broader repertoire of spelling knowledge [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### How spelling becomes more automatic and flexible

Spelling becomes more automatic and flexible as children transition from relying on phonological strategies to using orthographic and morphological knowledge. The evidence says that stage theory holds that children internalize orthographic features in a hierarchical, developmental progression, tending to master specific spelling features in a predictable order [N5-F3]. It also says that stage theory views spelling development as a hierarchical progression in which children gradually internalize more complex spelling patterns [N5-F3].  

Later, the overlapping waves model is presented as an alternative that emphasizes gradual change, adaptive choice, and a broad repertoire of strategies [N5-F1]. This suggests that late spelling development becomes more flexible because children can draw on multiple strategies rather than relying on a single strategy at a time [N5-F1]. The evidence also says that spelling knowledge provides the foundation for efficient encoding and decoding, giving individuals more room for thinking and planning [N5-F3].  

So, late spelling is characterized by increased fluency, rule application, and flexibility. Children move from effortful, strategy-dependent spelling to more automatic spelling that can be used flexibly across different contexts [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that spelling ability is tied to reading and writing efficiency, implying that late spelling is not just a matter of accuracy but also of cognitive flexibility [N5-F3].

## Theoretical and alternative explanations of spelling development mini-report

### Stage theory vs repertoire/wave theory

The evidence identifies two major theoretical perspectives in spelling research: **stage theory** and **repertoire/alternative theories** [N5-R1][N7-R1][N7-R3]. Stage theory holds that learners follow a developmental progression reflecting the increasing complexity of the spelling system itself [N5-F2]. Repertoire/alternative theories, by contrast, suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. The 2020 article on spelling and reading explicitly contrasts these two views and states that repertoire theory and similar alternative perspectives have emerged in response to stage theory [N5-F2].  

A later source describes the debate as follows: stage theory suggests learners follow a developmental progression reflecting increasing spelling-system complexity, whereas repertoire theorists suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information throughout development [N7-R3]. This contrast is central to understanding how spelling progression is explained.

### How each framework explains spelling progression

**Stage theory** explains spelling progression as a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages, with each stage dominated by different sources of knowledge and different strategies [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence states that stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also describes transitions as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].  

**Repertoire/alternative theories**, by contrast, emphasize a broader, more flexible learning framework. The evidence notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives suggest learners can understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. It also says that these perspectives emphasize a broad repertoire of spelling strategies, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. The overlapping waves model is described as a framework based on abundant variability, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. In this view, children develop a broad repertoire of spelling strategies and can adaptively choose among them, with gradual shifts in strategy use over time [N5-F1].  

The evidence also notes that repertoire and wave theories do not assume a consistent and static use of only one strategy at a time [N5-F1]. Instead, they endorse multiple strategies and shifts in strategy performance, while stage theory assumes a single dominant strategy per stage [N5-F1]. This is a key distinction: stage theory is about qualitative stage changes, whereas repertoire/wave theories are about continuous, flexible, and gradually changing strategy use [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Which evidence supports or challenges stage-based models

The evidence strongly supports stage-based models as a central framework for spelling development. The Dutch study explicitly says that stage theories of spelling development are part of the modal aspects of the field and that they describe a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages [N6-R3]. The core developmental spelling model also repeatedly identifies the same five stages and describes transitions between them as qualitative changes in strategy and information use [N1-F1].  

However, the evidence also challenges stage-based models by highlighting limitations. One source notes that a stage description of spelling development may not fully capture the complexity of learning to spell [N1-F1]. Another source says that the depth of children’s knowledge of the spelling system and the variety of knowledge sources and strategies they can use are not fully accounted for in stage approaches [N1-F1]. A separate source says that some researchers argue that variability in strategy use is better described in terms of overlapping waves rather than stage-like models [N1-F1].  

The 2020 article on spelling and reading adds that stage theory has been a predominant perspective in spelling research for many years, but alternative theorists challenge it by arguing that learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information throughout development [N5-F2]. The same article notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives have emerged as responses to stage theory [N5-F2].  

So the evidence supports stage theory as a useful explanatory framework for the developmental sequence of spelling, while also challenging it by emphasizing complexity, flexibility, and strategy variability [N1-F1][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The strongest support for stage theory comes from its historical prevalence and the consistent identification of the five-stage progression [N1-F1][N6-R3], while the strongest challenge comes from repertoire/wave theories and longitudinal evidence showing gradual, flexible strategy development [N5-F1][N5-F2].

## How the developmental spelling model explains children’s progression through spelling stages

The developmental spelling model explains children’s spelling progression as a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages, each representing a different way children represent words, use spelling knowledge, and rely on different strategies [N1-F1][N5-F2]. In other words, the model is not simply about spelling getting more accurate over time; it is about spelling becoming more systematic, rule-based, and conventionally grounded [N1-F1]. The evidence repeatedly identifies the same five-stage sequence: precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional/morphemic, and correct [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. This structure is central to the model’s explanation of development.

### The core developmental sequence: five stages in order

The model organizes spelling development into five recognizable stages:

1. **Precommunicative stage**  
2. **Semiphonetic stage**  
3. **Phonetic stage**  
4. **Transitional or morphemic stage**  
5. **Correct stage** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]

Some sources describe the final stage as “dictionary” spelling or the “correct stage,” while others use slightly different phrasing, such as “emergent invented spelling” [N1-R1][N1-R2]. Regardless of phrasing, the model is best understood as a developmental sequence in which spelling becomes progressively more systematic [N1-F1][N1-R1].

### What each stage represents developmentally

Each stage reflects a qualitative shift in how children represent spelling and use spelling knowledge.

- **Precommunicative stage**: Children combine letters and letter-like symbols in a relatively haphazard manner without systematic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences [N1-F1].  
- **Semiphonetic stage**: Children use knowledge of letter names to spell, but their written word representations do not yet constitute a complete mapping of the sound structures of words [N1-F1].  
- **Phonetic stage**: The sound-out strategy is characteristic: all of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but children do not yet show full knowledge of orthographic conventions [N1-F1].  
- **Transitional/morphemic stage**: Children demonstrate growing knowledge of basic spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations in their spellings [N1-F1].  
- **Correct stage**: Children master phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects of spelling competence [N1-F1].  

This progression shows increasing sophistication: from arbitrary mark-making through letter-name use, to sound-based spelling, to spelling that incorporates patterns, conventions, and morphology, and finally to conventional, rule-based spelling [N1-F1]. The model also notes that some stage theories do not subsume a qualitatively different “correct” stage, recognizing that correctly spelled words are not necessarily spelled using qualitatively different information and strategies from incorrectly spelled words [N1-F1]. Still, the common core of stage theory is a transition from phonological dependence toward orthographic and morphological mastery [N1-F1].

### How the model explains transitions between stages

The model explains transitions as qualitative changes in strategy and information use. In the precommunicative stage, children rely on arbitrary or haphazard letter combinations, whereas later stages become increasingly systematic [N1-F1]. Stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also says that transitions are conceptualized as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].

A key point is that each stage is labeled by the predominant information and strategies used at that stage [N1-F1]. This means the model is not simply a linear increase in accuracy; it is a sequence of qualitatively different phases, each with its own dominant knowledge source and strategy [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that stage theory holds that children internalize orthographic features in a hierarchical, developmental progression, tending to master specific spelling features in a predictable order [N5-F3]. This supports the idea that transitions are not abrupt but are embedded in a broader developmental progression [N5-F3].

### Early spelling development: letter-name and letter-sound knowledge emerge first

Early spelling development begins with children learning to associate letter names with sounds. The evidence states that children progress through stages where knowledge of letter names and letter-sound correspondences becomes central [N1-F1]. In the semiphonetic stage, children use knowledge of letter names to spell, but their written word representations do not yet fully map sound structures [N1-F1]. A separate source on early spelling development notes that children start making marks and scribbles at around 1–2 years old, and that prephonological and phonological stages are early parts of this process [N2-R5].

This suggests that letter-name knowledge emerges before letter-sound knowledge becomes systematic. In the semiphonetic stage, letter names are used, but the mapping to sound is incomplete [N1-F1]. Later, as phonetic spelling develops, children begin to represent more of the sound structure of words [N1-F1]. So the progression is from name-based mark-making to more sound-based spelling [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### What early spelling attempts look like

Early spelling attempts are described as invented spelling and mark-making. One source says children progress from precommunicative through invented spelling to accurate dictionary spelling [N1-R1]. Another source similarly describes the five stages as including invented spelling [N1-R2][N1-R3]. The same evidence describes the precommunicative stage as combining letters and letter-like symbols in a relatively haphazard manner [N1-F1]. A separate early-spelling source says children start making marks and scribbles on surfaces at around 1–2 years old, and that mark-making “make meaning” [N2-R5].

In the semiphonetic stage, children use letter names to spell, but their spellings do not yet fully represent word sounds [N1-F1]. In the phonetic stage, the sound-out strategy is characteristic: all of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but orthographic conventions are still not fully mastered [N1-F1]. So early spelling attempts can range from arbitrary scribbles and invented spellings through increasingly sound-driven but still inconsistent spellings [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R5].

### Why children struggle with early spelling

Children struggle with early spelling because their spelling systems are still developing and not yet fully aligned with the conventions of the writing system. In the precommunicative stage, letter combinations are arbitrary and lack systematic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences [N1-F1]. In the semiphonetic stage, children use letter names, but their written representations do not yet map sound structures fully [N1-F1]. In the phonetic stage, they can represent all sounds, but orthographic conventions remain weak [N1-F1].  

The evidence also notes that some stage theories do not subsume a qualitatively different “correct” stage, recognizing that correctly spelled words are not necessarily spelled using qualitatively different information and strategies from incorrectly spelled words [N1-F1]. This implies that early spelling struggles are not just about getting the right letters, but about coordinating multiple knowledge sources—letter names, sounds, and orthographic conventions—that children are still learning to integrate [N1-F1].  

In short, early spelling struggles stem from incomplete knowledge of letter-sound correspondences, inconsistent use of letter names, and limited orthographic awareness [N1-F1][N2-R5]. These limitations are developmentally normal and reflect the transition from precommunicative mark-making to more systematic spelling [N1-R1][N1-F1].

### Intermediate spelling development: phonetic spelling and spelling patterns emerge

Intermediate spelling development is marked by the emergence of phonetic spelling and the beginnings of spelling patterns. Phonetic spelling emerges as children begin to represent the sounds of words more systematically. The evidence states that the sound-out strategy is characteristic of the third spelling stage: all of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but children do not yet show full knowledge of orthographic conventions [N1-F1]. A related source says that during the phonetic stage, children between the ages of 5–7 have a better understanding of phonetics and can spell words based on that understanding [N3-R2].  

This means phonetic spelling develops from semiphonetic letter-name use to a more consistent, if still imperfect, representation of sounds. It is not yet fully conventional spelling, but it reflects a qualitative shift toward sound-based word representation [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that phonetic spelling is part of a broader developmental sequence that eventually includes spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphology [N1-F1].

### What spelling patterns children begin to use

As spelling moves beyond phonetic stage, children begin to use spelling patterns rather than relying solely on sound-out strategies. The evidence describes the transitional or morphemic stage as one where children demonstrate growing knowledge of basic spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations in their spellings [N1-F1]. A separate source identifies the stage sequence as including patterns within-words and syllable juncture [N3-R3]. Another source notes that teaching spelling of specific patterns and groups is much more effective than testing mixed patterns for a single sound or phonetically [N3-R5].  

This suggests that intermediate spelling development involves learning common letter patterns and morphological structures. Children start to recognize recurring spellings and the relationships between word parts, such as prefixes, suffixes, and base words [N1-F1][N3-R3]. These patterns are not yet fully conventionalized, but they represent a shift from sound-driven spelling to rule-like or pattern-based spelling [N1-F1][N3-R5].

### How accuracy and consistency improve

Accuracy and consistency improve as children move from phonetic spelling toward transitional/morphemic spelling. In the phonetic stage, children represent all sounds, but orthographic conventions are still weak [N1-F1]. In the transitional stage, children begin to show more consistent use of spelling patterns and orthographic conventions [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that longitudinal studies of spelling development are relevant because they examine how spelling skills change over time [N6-R3].  

This implies that accuracy and consistency do not improve uniformly. Children may initially produce many phonetically plausible but incorrect spellings, and then gradually integrate more conventional spellings and patterns [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The empirical evidence also supports a developmental sequence in which spelling becomes more systematic and less arbitrary as children gain more knowledge of spelling patterns and orthographic rules [N6-R3][N1-F1].

### Late spelling development: conventional spelling becomes dominant

Late spelling development is characterized by the emergence of conventional spelling and the dominance of orthographic and morphological knowledge. The evidence states that the transitional stage demonstrates growing knowledge of spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations [N1-F1]. The correct stage is described as when phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects of spelling competence are mastered [N1-F1]. A related source notes that the transitional stage reflects an emerging understanding of conventional spelling patterns and phonics rules, with vowels being a particular focus [N4-R4].  

This means conventional spelling becomes dominant gradually, not suddenly. It becomes dominant as children internalize orthographic rules and use them alongside morphological knowledge [N1-F1][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that spelling becomes more accurate and conventional as children move from phonetic to transitional spelling [N1-F1]. In other words, late spelling is characterized by the increasing use of established spelling conventions rather than arbitrary or purely phonetic spellings [N1-F1][N4-R4].

### What spelling rules children learn

Children learn spelling rules related to orthography, morphology, and phonics. The evidence notes that the transitional stage involves growing knowledge of spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations [N1-F1]. It also says that the correct stage is when phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects are mastered [N1-F1]. A separate source on late spelling development states that the transitional stage reflects an emerging understanding of conventional spelling patterns and phonics rules [N4-R4].  

These rules include both surface orthographic conventions and deeper morphological rules. Children learn to apply rules for silent letters, doubling consonants, vowel patterns, and word parts [N1-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that spelling knowledge is not limited to one source; it includes phonological, orthographic, and morphological information [N5-F2]. This supports the idea that late spelling is not just about memorizing isolated rules, but about using a broader repertoire of spelling knowledge [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### How spelling becomes more automatic and flexible

Spelling becomes more automatic and flexible as children transition from relying on phonological strategies to using orthographic and morphological knowledge. The evidence says that stage theory holds that children internalize orthographic features in a hierarchical, developmental progression, tending to master specific spelling features in a predictable order [N5-F3]. It also says that stage theory views spelling development as a hierarchical progression in which children gradually internalize more complex spelling patterns [N5-F3].  

Later, the overlapping waves model is presented as an alternative that emphasizes gradual change, adaptive choice, and a broad repertoire of strategies [N5-F1]. This suggests that late spelling development becomes more flexible because children can draw on multiple strategies rather than relying on a single strategy at a time [N5-F1]. The evidence also says that spelling knowledge provides the foundation for efficient encoding and decoding, giving individuals more room for thinking and planning [N5-F3].  

So, late spelling is characterized by increased fluency, rule application, and flexibility. Children move from effortful, strategy-dependent spelling to more automatic spelling that can be used flexibly across different contexts [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that spelling ability is tied to reading and writing efficiency, implying that late spelling is not just a matter of accuracy but also of cognitive flexibility [N5-F3].

### Theoretical context: stage theory vs repertoire/wave theories

The evidence identifies two major theoretical perspectives in spelling research: **stage theory** and **repertoire/alternative theories** [N5-R1][N7-R1][N7-R3]. Stage theory holds that learners follow a developmental progression reflecting the increasing complexity of the spelling system itself [N5-F2]. Repertoire/alternative theories, by contrast, suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. The 2020 article on spelling and reading explicitly contrasts these two views and states that repertoire theory and similar alternative perspectives have emerged in response to stage theory [N5-F2].  

A later source describes the debate as follows: stage theory suggests learners follow a developmental progression reflecting increasing spelling-system complexity, whereas repertoire theorists suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information throughout development [N7-R3]. This contrast is central to understanding how spelling progression is explained.

### How each framework explains spelling progression

**Stage theory** explains spelling progression as a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages, with each stage dominated by different sources of knowledge and different strategies [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence states that stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also describes transitions as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].  

**Repertoire/alternative theories**, by contrast, emphasize a broader, more flexible learning framework. The evidence notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives suggest learners can understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. It also says that these perspectives emphasize a broad repertoire of spelling strategies, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. The overlapping waves model is described as a framework based on abundant variability, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. In this view, children develop a broad repertoire of spelling strategies and can adaptively choose among them, with gradual shifts in strategy use over time [N5-F1].  

The evidence also notes that repertoire and wave theories do not assume a consistent and static use of only one strategy at a time [N5-F1]. Instead, they endorse multiple strategies and shifts in strategy performance, while stage theory assumes a single dominant strategy per stage [N5-F1]. This is a key distinction: stage theory is about qualitative stage changes, whereas repertoire/wave theories are about continuous, flexible, and gradually changing strategy use [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Which evidence supports or challenges stage-based models

The evidence strongly supports stage-based models as a central framework for spelling development. The Dutch study explicitly says that stage theories of spelling development are part of the modal aspects of the field and that they describe a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages [N6-R3]. The core developmental spelling model also repeatedly identifies the same five stages and describes transitions between them as qualitative changes in strategy and information use [N1-F1].  

However, the evidence also challenges stage-based models by highlighting limitations. One source notes that a stage description of spelling development may not fully capture the complexity of learning to spell [N1-F1]. Another source says that the depth of children’s knowledge of the spelling system and the variety of knowledge sources and strategies they can use are not fully accounted for in stage approaches [N1-F1]. A separate source says that some researchers argue that variability in strategy use is better described in terms of overlapping waves rather than stage-like models [N1-F1].  

The 2020 article on spelling and reading adds that stage theory has been a predominant perspective in spelling research for many years, but alternative theorists challenge it by arguing that learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information throughout development [N5-F2]. The same article notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives have emerged as responses to stage theory [N5-F2].  

So the evidence supports stage theory as a useful explanatory framework for the developmental sequence of spelling, while also challenging it by emphasizing complexity, flexibility, and strategy variability [N1-F1][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The strongest support for stage theory comes from its historical prevalence and the consistent identification of the five-stage progression [N1-F1][N6-R3], while the strongest challenge comes from repertoire/wave theories and longitudinal evidence showing gradual, flexible strategy development [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the developmental spelling model explains children’s progression through spelling stages as a sequence of qualitatively distinct phases: from arbitrary mark-making and letter-name use, through phonetic spelling, to spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and finally conventional spelling [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. Each stage reflects a different dominant source of knowledge and strategy, and transitions are explained as discontinuous and multidimensional shifts rather than smooth linear improvement [N1-F1][N5-F2].  

Early spelling struggles are rooted in incomplete letter-sound knowledge and weak orthographic awareness [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Intermediate spelling improves accuracy and consistency as children use phonetic spelling and then begin to apply spelling patterns [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R3]. Late spelling becomes more conventional, rule-based, and flexible, with spelling knowledge tied to reading and writing efficiency [N1-F1][N4-R4][N5-F3].  

Theoretical context is important: stage theory provides a clear developmental sequence, while repertoire/wave theories challenge it by emphasizing flexibility, strategy variability, and gradual change [N5-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence supports stage theory as a major explanatory framework, but also suggests that spelling development is best understood as a complex, flexible process rather than a simple series of fixed stages [N1-F1][N5-F1][N5-F2].

## Core developmental spelling model mini-report

The developmental spelling model presented in the evidence is broadly stage-based, with several authors identifying a five-stage progression. One source states that children progress through five stages of spelling development, from precommunicative through invented spelling to accurate dictionary spelling [N1-R1]. Another source explicitly names the same five-phase sequence: precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional, and correct [N1-R2]. A third source also lists the five stages as precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional, and correct [N1-R3], while a fourth source describes the Bear, Invernizzi, Templeton & Johnston model as an overview of the five stages [N1-R4]. A fifth source notes that Gentry’s model also outlines a five-phase progression [N1-R5]. Across these sources, the core model is therefore best summarized as a five-stage developmental sequence.

### Which stages are recognized in the model?

The most consistent stage sequence across the evidence is:

1. **Precommunicative stage**  
2. **Semiphonetic stage**  
3. **Phonetic stage**  
4. **Transitional or morphemic stage**  
5. **Correct stage** [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]

Some sources use slightly different phrasing, such as “emergent invented spelling” instead of “precommunicative” [N1-R1], and some describe the final stage as “dictionary” spelling or the “correct stage” [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The empirical Dutch study also notes that both Gentry (1982) and Ehri, 1986, 1992 have distinguished these five stages [N1-F1].

### What each stage represents developmentally

Each stage marks a qualitative shift in how children represent spelling and use spelling knowledge:

- **Precommunicative stage**: Children combine letters and letter-like symbols in a relatively haphazard manner without systematic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences [N1-F1].  
- **Semiphonetic stage**: Children use knowledge of letter names to spell, but their written word representations do not yet constitute a complete mapping of the sound structures of words [N1-F1].  
- **Phonetic stage**: The sound-out strategy is characteristic: all of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but children do not yet show full knowledge of orthographic conventions [N1-F1].  
- **Transitional/morphemic stage**: Children demonstrate growing knowledge of basic spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations in their spellings [N1-F1].  
- **Correct stage**: Children master phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects of spelling competence [N1-F1].  

This developmental sequence reflects increasing sophistication: from arbitrary mark-making through letter-name use, to phonetic spelling, to spelling that incorporates patterns, conventions, and morphology, and finally to conventional, rule-based spelling [N1-F1].

### How the model explains transitions between stages

The stage model explains transitions as qualitative changes in the use of strategy and information. In the precommunicative stage, children rely on arbitrary or haphazard letter combinations, whereas later stages become increasingly systematic [N1-F1]. Stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also says that transitions are conceptualized as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].  

A key theoretical point is that each stage is labeled by the predominant information and strategies used at that stage [N1-F1]. This means the model does not treat spelling as a smooth, linear increase in accuracy alone, but as a sequence of qualitatively distinct phases where different knowledge sources and strategies dominate [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that some stage theories do not subsume a qualitatively different “correct” stage, recognizing that correctly spelled words are not necessarily spelled using qualitatively different information and strategies [N1-F1]. Still, the common core of stage theory is a transition from phonological dependence toward orthographic and morphological mastery [N1-F1].

### Theoretical context

The evidence also emphasizes that stage theory is one of several perspectives in spelling research. The 2020 article on spelling and reading contrasts stage theory with repertoire/alternative theories, noting that stage theory suggests learners follow a developmental progression reflecting increasing complexity of the spelling system itself, whereas repertoire theories suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand more information throughout development [N5-F2]. This distinction is important because it shows that the developmental spelling model is not the only explanatory framework, and that stage theory is debated in the literature [N5-F2].  

Overall, the core developmental spelling model is a five-stage sequence: precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional/morphemic, and correct. Each stage represents a qualitative shift in spelling strategy and knowledge use, with transitions reflecting discontinuous, multidimensional developmental changes [N1-F1]. The model is supported by the repeated identification of these stages across sources, but the evidence also shows that it is contested by alternative views [N1-F1][N5-F2].

## Intermediate spelling development mini-report

### How phonetic spelling emerges and evolves

Phonetic spelling emerges as children begin to represent the sounds of words more systematically. As spelling moves beyond phonetic stage, children begin to use spelling patterns rather than relying solely on sound-out strategies. Children start to recognize recurring spellings and the relationships between word parts, such as prefixes, suffixes, and base words [N1-F1][N3-R3]. Accuracy and consistency improve as children move from phonetic spelling toward transitional/morphemic spelling. In the phonetic stage, children represent all sounds, but orthographic conventions are still weak [N1-F1]. ### Stage theory vs repertoire/wave theory

The evidence identifies two major theoretical perspectives in spelling research: **stage theory** and **repertoire/alternative theories** [N5-R1][N7-R1][N7-R3]. Stage theory holds that learners follow a developmental progression reflecting the increasing complexity of the spelling system itself [N5-F2]. Repertoire/alternative theories, by contrast, suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. The 2020 article on spelling and reading explicitly contrasts these two views and states that repertoire theory and similar alternative perspectives have emerged in response to stage theory [N5-F2].  

A later source describes the debate as follows: stage theory suggests learners follow a developmental progression reflecting increasing spelling-system complexity, whereas repertoire theorists suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information throughout development [N7-R3]. This contrast is central to understanding how spelling progression is explained.

### How each framework explains spelling progression

**Stage theory** explains spelling progression as a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages, with each stage dominated by different sources of knowledge and different strategies [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence states that stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also describes transitions as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].  

**Repertoire/alternative theories**, by contrast, emphasize a broader, more flexible learning framework. The evidence notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives suggest learners can understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. It also says that these perspectives emphasize a broad repertoire of spelling strategies, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. The overlapping waves model is described as a framework based on abundant variability, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. In this view, children develop a broad repertoire of spelling strategies and can adaptively choose among them, with gradual shifts in strategy use over time [N5-F1].  

The evidence also notes that repertoire and wave theories do not assume a consistent and static use of only one strategy at a time [N5-F1]. Instead, they endorse multiple strategies and shifts in strategy performance, while stage theory assumes a single dominant strategy per stage [N5-F1]. This is a key distinction: stage theory is about qualitative stage changes, whereas repertoire/wave theories are about continuous, flexible, and gradually changing strategy use [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Which evidence supports or challenges stage-based models

The evidence strongly supports stage-based models as a central framework for spelling development. The Dutch study explicitly says that stage theories of spelling development are part of the modal aspects of the field and that they describe a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages [N6-R3]. The core developmental spelling model also repeatedly identifies the same five stages and describes transitions between them as qualitative changes in strategy and information use [N1-F1].  

However, the evidence also challenges stage-based models by highlighting limitations. One source notes that a stage description of spelling development may not fully capture the complexity of learning to spell [N1-F1]. Another source says that the depth of children’s knowledge of the spelling system and the variety of knowledge sources and strategies they can use are not fully accounted for in stage approaches [N1-F1]. The 2020 article on spelling and reading adds that stage theory has been a predominant perspective in spelling research for many years, but alternative theorists challenge it by arguing that learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information throughout development [N5-F2]. The same article notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives have emerged as responses to stage theory [N5-F2].  

So the evidence supports stage theory as a useful explanatory framework for the developmental sequence of spelling, while also challenging it by emphasizing complexity, flexibility, and strategy variability [N1-F1][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The strongest support for stage theory comes from its historical prevalence and the consistent identification of the five-stage progression [N1-F1][N6-R3], while the strongest challenge comes from repertoire/wave theories and longitudinal evidence showing gradual, flexible strategy development [N5-F1][N5-F2].

## Core developmental spelling model mini-report

The developmental spelling model presented in the evidence is broadly stage-based, with several authors identifying a five-stage progression. One source states that children progress through five stages of spelling development, from precommunicative through invented spelling to accurate dictionary spelling [N1-R1]. Another source explicitly names the same five-phase sequence: precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional, and correct [N1-R2]. A third source also lists the five stages as precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional, and correct [N1-R3], while a fourth source describes the Bear, Invernizzi, Templeton & Johnston model as an overview of the five stages [N1-R4]. A fifth source notes that Gentry’s model also outlines a five-phase progression [N1-R5]. Across these sources, the core model is therefore best summarized as a five-stage developmental sequence.

### Which stages are recognized in the model?

The most consistent stage sequence across the evidence is:

1. **Precommunicative stage**  
2. **Semiphonetic stage**  
3. **Phonetic stage**  
4. **Transitional or morphemic stage**  
5. **Correct stage** [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]

Some sources use slightly different phrasing, such as “emergent invented spelling” instead of “precommunicative” [N1-R1], and some describe the final stage as “dictionary” spelling or the “correct stage” [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The empirical Dutch study also notes that both Gentry (1982) and Ehri, 1986, 1992 have distinguished these five stages [N1-F1].

### What each stage represents developmentally

Each stage marks a qualitative shift in how children represent spelling and use spelling knowledge:

- **Precommunicative stage**: Children combine letters and letter-like symbols in a relatively haphazard manner without systematic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences [N1-F1].  
- **Semiphonetic stage**: Children use knowledge of letter names to spell, but their written word representations do not yet constitute a complete mapping of the sound structures of words [N1-F1].  
- **Phonetic stage**: The sound-out strategy is characteristic: all of the sounds in a word are represented by letters, but children do not yet show full knowledge of orthographic conventions [N1-F1].  
- **Transitional/morphemic stage**: Children demonstrate growing knowledge of basic spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphological relations in their spellings [N1-F1].  
- **Correct stage**: Children master phonological, orthographic, and morphological aspects of spelling competence [N1-F1].  

This developmental sequence reflects increasing sophistication: from arbitrary mark-making through letter-name use, to phonetic spelling, to spelling that incorporates patterns, conventions, and morphology, and finally to conventional, rule-based spelling [N1-F1].

### How the model explains transitions between stages

The stage model explains transitions as qualitative changes in the use of strategy and information. In the precommunicative stage, children rely on arbitrary or haphazard letter combinations, whereas later stages become increasingly systematic [N1-F1]. Stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also says that transitions are conceptualized as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].  

A key theoretical point is that each stage is labeled by the predominant information and strategies used at that stage [N1-F1]. This means the model does not treat spelling as a smooth, linear increase in accuracy alone, but as a sequence of qualitatively distinct phases where different knowledge sources and strategies dominate [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that some stage theories do not subsume a qualitatively different “correct” stage, recognizing that correctly spelled words are not necessarily spelled using qualitatively different information and strategies [N1-F1]. Still, the common core of stage theory is a transition from phonological dependence toward orthographic and morphological mastery [N1-F1].

### Theoretical context

The evidence also emphasizes that stage theory is one of several perspectives in spelling research. The 2020 article on spelling and reading contrasts stage theory with repertoire/alternative theories, noting that stage theory suggests learners follow a developmental progression reflecting increasing complexity of the spelling system itself, whereas repertoire theories suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand more information throughout development [N5-F2]. This distinction is important because it shows that the developmental spelling model is not the only explanatory framework, and that stage theory is debated in the literature [N5-F2].  

Overall, the core developmental spelling model is a five-stage sequence: precommunicative, semiphonetic, phonetic, transitional/morphemic, and correct. Each stage represents a qualitative shift in spelling strategy and knowledge use, with transitions reflecting discontinuous, multidimensional developmental changes [N1-F1]. The model is supported by the repeated identification of these stages across sources, but the evidence also shows that it is contested by alternative views [N1-F1][N5-F2].

Children struggle with early spelling because their spelling systems are still developing and not yet fully aligned with the conventions of the writing system. In the precommunicative stage, letter combinations are arbitrary and lack systematic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences [N1-F1]. ### How phonetic spelling emerges and evolves

Phonetic spelling emerges as children begin to represent the sounds of words more systematically. The evidence also notes that phonetic spelling is part of a broader developmental sequence that eventually includes spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphology [N1-F1].

### What spelling patterns children begin to use

As spelling moves beyond phonetic stage, children begin to use spelling patterns rather than relying solely on sound-out strategies. Another source notes that teaching spelling of specific patterns and groups is more effective than testing mixed patterns for a single sound or phonetically [N3-R5].

Children start to recognize recurring spellings and the relationships between word parts, such as prefixes, suffixes, and base words [N1-F1][N3-R3]. These patterns are not yet fully conventionalized, but they represent a shift from sound-driven spelling to rule-like or pattern-based spelling [N1-F1][N3-R5].

Accuracy and consistency improve as children move from phonetic spelling toward transitional/morphemic spelling. Intermediate spelling development is marked by the emergence of phonetic spelling, followed by the use of spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and morphology. The evidence identifies two major theoretical perspectives in spelling research: **stage theory** and **repertoire/alternative theories** [N5-R1][N7-R1][N7-R3]. This contrast is central to understanding how spelling progression is explained.

### How each framework explains spelling progression

**Stage theory** explains spelling progression as a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages, with each stage dominated by different sources of knowledge and different strategies [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence states that stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also describes transitions as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].  

**Repertoire/alternative theories**, by contrast, emphasize a broader, more flexible learning framework. The evidence notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives suggest learners can understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. It also says that these perspectives emphasize a broad repertoire of spelling strategies, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. The overlapping waves model is described as a framework based on abundant variability, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. In this view, children develop a broad repertoire of spelling strategies and can adaptively choose among them, with gradual shifts in strategy use over time [N5-F1].  

The evidence also notes that repertoire and wave theories do not assume a consistent and static use of only one strategy at a time [N5-F1]. Instead, they endorse multiple strategies and shifts in strategy performance, while stage theory assumes a single dominant strategy per stage [N5-F1]. This is a key distinction: stage theory is about qualitative stage changes, whereas repertoire/wave theories are about continuous, flexible, and gradually changing strategy use [N5-F1][N5-F2].

The evidence strongly supports stage-based models as a central framework for spelling development. So the evidence supports stage theory as a useful explanatory framework for the developmental sequence of spelling, while also challenging it by emphasizing complexity, flexibility, and strategy variability [N1-F1][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The strongest support for stage theory comes from its historical prevalence and the consistent identification of the five-stage progression [N1-F1][N6-R3], while the strongest challenge comes from repertoire/wave theories and longitudinal evidence showing gradual, flexible strategy development [N5-F1][N5-F2].

Children move from effortful, strategy-dependent spelling to more automatic spelling that can be used flexibly across different contexts [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that spelling ability is tied to reading and writing efficiency, implying that late spelling is not just a matter of accuracy but also of cognitive flexibility [N5-F3].

### Theoretical context: stage theory vs repertoire/wave theories

The evidence identifies two major theoretical perspectives in spelling research: **stage theory** and **repertoire/alternative theories** [N5-R1][N7-R1][N7-R3]. Stage theory holds that learners follow a developmental progression reflecting the increasing complexity of the spelling system itself [N5-F2]. Repertoire/alternative theories, by contrast, suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. The 2020 article on spelling and reading explicitly contrasts these two views and states that repertoire theory and similar alternative perspectives have emerged in response to stage theory [N5-F2].  

A later source describes the debate as follows: stage theory suggests learners follow a developmental progression reflecting increasing spelling-system complexity, whereas repertoire theorists suggest learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information throughout development [N7-R3]. This contrast is central to understanding how spelling progression is explained.

### How each framework explains spelling progression

**Stage theory** explains spelling progression as a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages, with each stage dominated by different sources of knowledge and different strategies [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence states that stage theory proposes that children move from relying on phonological properties to recognizing and representing orthographic and morphological regularities and rules [N1-F1]. It also describes transitions as discontinuous and multidimensional, with children spelling words fundamentally differently in successive stages [N1-F1].  

**Repertoire/alternative theories**, by contrast, emphasize a broader, more flexible learning framework. The evidence notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives suggest learners can understand much more information about the spelling system throughout development [N5-F2]. It also says that these perspectives emphasize a broad repertoire of spelling strategies, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. The overlapping waves model is described as a framework based on abundant variability, adaptive choice, and gradual change [N5-F1]. In this view, children develop a broad repertoire of spelling strategies and can adaptively choose among them, with gradual shifts in strategy use over time [N5-F1].  

The evidence also notes that repertoire and wave theories do not assume a consistent and static use of only one strategy at a time [N5-F1]. Instead, they endorse multiple strategies and shifts in strategy performance, while stage theory assumes a single dominant strategy per stage [N5-F1]. This is a key distinction: stage theory is about qualitative stage changes, whereas repertoire/wave theories are about continuous, flexible, and gradually changing strategy use [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Which evidence supports or challenges stage-based models

The evidence strongly supports stage-based models as a central framework for spelling development. The Dutch study explicitly says that stage theories of spelling development are part of the modal aspects of the field and that they describe a sequence of qualitatively distinct stages [N6-R3]. The core developmental spelling model also repeatedly identifies the same five stages and describes transitions between them as qualitative changes in strategy and information use [N1-F1].  

However, the evidence also challenges stage-based models by highlighting limitations. One source notes that a stage description of spelling development may not fully capture the complexity of learning to spell [N1-F1]. Another source says that the depth of children’s knowledge of the spelling system and the variety of knowledge sources and strategies they can use are not fully accounted for in stage approaches [N1-F1]. A separate source says that some researchers argue that variability in strategy use is better described in terms of overlapping waves rather than stage-like models [N1-F1].  

The 2020 article on spelling and reading adds that stage theory has been a predominant perspective in spelling research for many years, but alternative theorists challenge it by arguing that learners do not follow a linear progression and instead understand much more information throughout development [N5-F2]. The same article notes that repertoire theory and similar perspectives have emerged as responses to stage theory [N5-F2].  

So the evidence supports stage theory as a useful explanatory framework for the developmental sequence of spelling, while also challenging it by emphasizing complexity, flexibility, and strategy variability [N1-F1][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The strongest support for stage theory comes from its historical prevalence and the consistent identification of the five-stage progression [N1-F1][N6-R3], while the strongest challenge comes from repertoire/wave theories and longitudinal evidence showing gradual, flexible strategy development [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the developmental spelling model explains children’s progression through spelling stages as a sequence of qualitatively distinct phases: from arbitrary mark-making and letter-name use, through phonetic spelling, to spelling patterns, orthographic conventions, and finally conventional spelling [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. Each stage reflects a different dominant source of knowledge and strategy, and transitions are explained as discontinuous and multidimensional shifts rather than smooth linear improvement [N1-F1][N5-F2].  

Early spelling struggles are rooted in incomplete letter-sound knowledge and weak orthographic awareness [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Intermediate spelling improves accuracy and consistency as children use phonetic spelling and then begin to apply spelling patterns [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R3]. Late spelling becomes more conventional, rule-based, and flexible, with spelling knowledge tied to reading and writing efficiency [N1-F1][N4-R4][N5-F3].  

Theoretical context is important: stage theory provides a clear developmental sequence, while repertoire/wave theories challenge it by emphasizing flexibility, strategy variability, and gradual change [N5-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence supports stage theory as a major explanatory framework, but also suggests that spelling development is best understood as a complex, flexible process rather than a simple series of fixed stages [N1-F1][N5-F1][N5-F2].
